newsitem.title: JAPAN: Two Hong Kong activists still on Japan patrol boat.
newsitem.headline: Two Hong Kong activists still on Japan patrol boat.

text.p: Three Hong Kong and Taiwanese activists risked their lives on Monday when they jumped from their own pitching boats on to Japanese coastguard vessels in a high seas standoff over ownership of disputed islands.

A Japanese spokesman said after hours of cat-and-mouse games, including several slight collisions, a flotilla of about 20 Hong Kong and Taiwanese boats abandoned efforts to break through a coastguard cordon and land on the islands.
The dispute is over islands called the Senkakus in Japanese and the Diaoyus in Chinese, which are about equidistant between Taiwan and Japan's southern island chain of Okinawa.
The spokesman said two Hong Kong activists who jumped from a boat called "Protect-the-Diaoyus", flagship of the flotilla, on to a coastguard ship were still on board the Japanese ship.
A third protester who leapt from a Taiwanese boat on to another coastguard ship was returned to the flotilla, the spokesman said.
None of the three were arrested or detained in any way, said the spokesman.

"The two activists still on board our ship are highly excited," he told Reuters. "We tried to have them transferred back to the Protect-the-Diaoyus but the ship ignored our calls and just sailed away in the direction of Taiwan," he said.
The two will be handed over to one of the protest ships as soon as possible, the spokesman said.

The 20-strong Hong Kong-Taiwan flotilla, led by the Protect-the-Diaoyus, was on a protest manoeuvre near the uninhabited islands in the East China Sea when they were blocked by a fleet of about 60 Japanese coastguard vessels.
The spokesman said there were a few cases of ships from the two sides bumping each other but none of the ships suffered serious damage.
He said some protest ships entered 12-nautical mile territorial waters claimed by Japan but none were seized, as top Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama had warned.
"The Japanese government will take appropriate measures to block (the activists) from landing on the islands," government spokesman Kajiyama told a news conference earlier in the day.
Asked if the measures could include seizing the ships, Kajiyama replied: "Yes, that's right."
"As we have repeatedly said, the islands are Japan's territory and they are effectively controlled by Japan," Kajiyama said.
"Therefore, landing on the islands would constitute a violation of Japan's law."
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters: "We must not let them into our territorial waters."

The dispute over sovereignty has ignited fiery nationalist passions in Chinese communities in Hong Kong and Taiwan since a Japanese right-wing group built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the islands in July 1996.
A Hong Kong activist drowned in September when he jumped from a protest boat into stormy waters during an abortive voyage to the islands.

In a move that added fuel to the fire, four Japanese, including one legislator, planted a Japanese flag on one of the islands earlier this month and spent two hours surveying and holding a memorial ceremony.
Japan took over the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895. China and Taiwan say they should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
